#9596. 6 User Mindsets That Should Shape Your B2B Onboarding Strategy

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

Product Builder, hands on AI Developer. Spent a good part of the last 15 years building eCommerce Marketplaces (Zalando, eBay, Flipkart).

A field guide to B2B onboarding, with fixes you can ship this week.

For a moment, let’s put ourselves in the shoes of a classic B2B user, say a seller on an e-commerce platform. What do you think they really care about?

Sure, some users may care about some of those things, but only as a means to an end. At the crux, they care about two things:

And onboarding is the first place they find out whether you’ll deliver on either.

How do we make the first touchpoint that they go through easier, and focused on reaching their goals? We’ll focus on six mindsets users move through during onboarding.

Many B2B users normally need to view videos like this one to understand how to onboard themselves onto a platform. And it’s easy to see why: (a) the flows are complex; (b) if they need help, they really don’t know how to get it; and (c) the user can’t afford to get it wrong, or they lose several days.

1. Focus on one thing at a time. Onboarding is stressful, and it’s important for B2B SaaS firms to get the user’s focus on the one thing they need to get right at that point. Hide everything else. It can come later.

2. Make the flow as simple as it can be. If it isn’t yet, try again. For an ecommerce platform, its users are likely to have their catalog someplace, maybe just not in the exact format you need. Can you work with that? Or their catalog is already on their website. Can you pick it up from there?

If you are dealing with documents, can you pick up everything by just asking for the user’s Google Drive folder?

Agents are now good enough to not just do a read, but also an adversarial check of the data with 2–3 sources (public information, their site, etc.). Use them. Don’t overload the user with things you can take off their plate.

3. If something is complex, explain it right there. For example, show where the user can find their VAT ID, or where to get the compliance reference note for a product they are selling. How the app communicates that becomes truly crucial. Minimising mental blocks is more important for procedural cases than a smooth experience everywhere else.

The help should always be inline, exactly when the user is facing it, not elsewhere.

4. Answer the broader questions too. Sometimes the user’s question is more tangential, and broader than a specific field. For example: “How long would it take me to get started?” Or: “I am missing my VAT ID. How long is it likely to take me to get it, and how can I apply for it?” Being able to truly assist users with broader questions is where a bot can be really helpful. Not for all queries (most should be inline), but for a few cases.

5. Make mistakes easy to fix. It’s very underrated, and excruciatingly boring. But the biggest level of stress is when the user submits an error, and correcting it requires someone to “invalidate the form” and get back to them. Mistakes happen, and most of them are technically reversible. Allow users to edit their details at any point in time, so that they can proceed with confidence the first time around.

Try this week: Pick your three most-asked support questions and answer each one inline, on the screen where it comes up.

Offering an MCP connection is now non-negotiable. At Linear, issues created through MCP recently overtook those created in the app itself.

“This is the first week in Linear’s history when issues created through MCP surpassed application created ones.” — Jori Lallo, Linear, on X

And it should include onboarding itself: let users share their company details, upload their catalog or ask about their VAT ID without leaving Claude.

That said, not every user will come through MCP yet. Non-technical users may still prefer the stability of a guided workflow, and being shown how to scale.

Offer both, at least for the next 1–2 years.

Try this week: Expose one onboarding step (company details or catalog upload) as an MCP tool, then complete it from Claude yourself.

Using a B2B provider is often a multi-level game. A user’s end goal is a robust and steady income stream, or continuous compliance, or tracking, or a specific service like document signing. But each step builds on how well they did the previous one. So at every step, tell them what’s likely to work and what isn’t, from both a user and a commercial standpoint, before they have to ask.

Try this week: Pick the first milestone in your users’ journey and show them a progress signal for it, like “8 of 10 products ready to sell”.

When most companies talk about AI, what they do is add a chatbot on the side, which allows users to get information about any part of the site. That’s talking about AI, not using it. And users can hate it when a capability is oversold.

Product marketing matters, but in most cases you need to let your product do the talking. Too much talk and too little delivery just teach customers to tune you out, right when you have something worth saying.

Try this week: Find one “AI-powered” label in your onboarding and replace it with the outcome it delivers, e.g. “We’ve pre-filled 14 of 16 fields from your website.”

Say a user has a need the product doesn’t solve yet. They could wait for the next check-in with their account manager to raise it. Better: they can share it right away, from the screen they’re on. Better still: they get a real response, not a boilerplate “it’s on our roadmap”. And when their feedback does change something, tell them: “You asked, we shipped.” Show them you’re really listening.

New users see friction your team stopped noticing months ago. Onboarding is when their feedback is most valuable, and least likely to be collected.

Try this week: Add a one-line feedback box to your onboarding screens, and reply personally to every message for a week.

So design onboarding for roles, not accounts. Most onboarding treats the account as one person. Ask who’s signing up, show each person the steps and indicators that matter to them, and let them switch views when they need to.

Try this week: Add one question to signup (“What’s your role?”) and hide the steps that don’t apply to that role.

Onboarding is the first real touchpoint you have with your customer. It’s where they decide whether you care about them, or only about your own business. Sure, you care about that too. But they need to see that you care about them as users, as people, and about what they’re trying to achieve.

Keep these six mindsets in mind, and check that each one delivers the right level of value:

None of this needs a new AI feature. It needs onboarding designed for the person on the other side of the screen.

#9595. New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation

NVIDIA Cosmos world model development platform adds four new open-weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family for generating interactive world simulation and multi-sensor multi-view driving scenes:

All four models are post-trained examples of Cosmos 3 Nano and have 16B trainable parameters. The models use OpenMDW1.1, permitting commercial and non-commercial use under its terms.

Download the checkpoints · Read the technical report . Watch the demos

🦾 Robotics needs environments that can answer this across changing scenes and viewpoints. These checkpoints offer complementary ways to build them: Sim-Bimanual predicts visual consequences from actions, while Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator’s controls into generated observations.

🚦 For autonomous driving, appearance and geometry must agree. Synchronized camera and LiDAR generation connects visual observations with 3D sensing. Scene and traffic-signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, then study how a driving policy responds.

🔄 Each observation can shape the next action. Streaming generation connects video prediction to ongoing interaction, giving world-model researchers a way to explore how actions and observations unfold together.

🌐 An open foundation for others to build on. NVIDIA’s vision is to help researchers and developers create richer, more responsive simulated worlds. Open weights and post-training recipes provide a shared starting point for adapting models, comparing methods, and contributing improvements. These problems remain hard: the work ahead is to measure where the models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short.

Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data generation. It generates synchronized video across up to 11 camera views, including fisheyes, and supports joint RGB–LiDAR generation. Per-camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls specify scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance.

Developers can vary environmental conditions to expand training and evaluation coverage, with optional initial RGB images to anchor scene appearance. Joint LiDAR generation additionally uses aligned HD-map range-map controls. Transfer-Auto also serves as the foundation for adapting Cosmos to your own sensor rig and driving domain. Start by post-training it on your data to accommodate your camera layout, LiDAR configuration, and target environment. The adapted model can be used directly for offline data generation or undergo causal training and few-step distillation for fast streaming simulation—the development path used to create Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer-Auto. It generates successive small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in just a few denoising steps, using generated history and updated driving controls to support fast streaming and long, interactive rollouts.

Provide per-camera captions and synchronized WSM controls, optionally adding initial RGB images. For LiDAR generation, include HD-Map range controls aligned with the camera controls. The distilled model generates successive chunks using its rolling history. Closed-loop interaction requires a simulation runtime and WSM renderer to update those controls from driving inputs. For a new sensor rig or domain, adapt Transfer-Auto first, then distill it into Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto

Your simulator computes motion, contacts, and physical state. Sim-Transfer uses its spatial controls and a text prompt to render color observations that a policy can consume.

Action → simulator update → spatial controls → generated RGB → next policy action

Depth: relative distance from the camera.

Segmentation: regions and object boundaries.

Text guides appearance; physics and ground-truth state stay with the simulator.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer

Output Video From Sim-Bimanual Simulation Checkpoint

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual simulates how an environment evolves in response to a bimanual robot’s actions. It supports interactive two-arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controlled by a policy or human-operated joysticks.

Start with an image, move the robot or camera, and generate the next observations. One control sequence can switch between viewpoint changes and manipulation.

The mixed-action example uses 59 control values, padded to 64 during training. Its schema defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains. Follow those conventions so each value describes the intended motion.

Keep timing aligned: T transitions need T+1 observations. Training transforms raw captures into the model’s action representation; released inference actions are already normalized.

Here, Sim-Transfer generates visuals from a physics simulator’s updated state; Sim-Bimanual generates the next observation directly from the scene and robot actions.

Requirements: Linux, an NVIDIA GPU, Docker, and NVIDIA Container Toolkit. The published vLLM-Omni setup was tested on one GB200; this is not a minimum-memory specification. The server downloads weights; the clients fetch sample inputs.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual

Cosmos 3’s Mixture-of-Transformers backbone connects separate text-processing and visual-generation networks through attention. The generator predicts each short segment from the prompt, available controls, and generated history.

Controls + history → generate chunk → decode images → update history

Denoising refines noisy, compressed video representations into a segment. Temporal-causal attention lets it read available history and controls while blocking future target observations. A key/value cache retains attention information for the next prediction.

The model operates on compressed video representations called latents. After the initial image, each latent time step represents four RGB frames. Transfer predicts one step per chunk; the optimized Bimanual setup in the report predicts two. Smaller chunks let new controls affect generation more often.

Stage 0 — Bidirectional adaptation: learn the domain and its control-to-video relationships from complete recorded clips.

Stage 1 — Teacher forcing: predict each chunk from earlier recorded observations and available controls, with the clean answer and future targets masked out.

Stage 2 — Consistency distillation: use a frozen teacher to train a student that generates each chunk in four denoising steps.

Stage 3 — Self-forcing: train on the student’s generated history. A frozen teacher and an auxiliary score model supply the distribution-matching signal.

Why the final stage matters: a slightly mispredicted object becomes context for later frames, so errors can compound. Self-forcing exposes training to that generated history. Distillation and caching reduce the cost of producing each observation.

The post-training recipes start from Cosmos3-Nano or compatible base weights and cover all four stages. Keep full training checkpoints to resume; exported inference weights omit optimizer and other training state.

Transfer-auto: Post-train on your driving data to adapt to your sensor rig and domain, and generate offline synthetic data.

Sim-auto: Apply causal training and distillation to an adapted Transfer-Auto model for fast streaming simulation.

Sim-Transfer : Post-train the checkpoint for your environment with local data preparation, stage configurations, and resume.

Sim-Bimanual: Post-train for your embodiment with data validation, stage configurations, checkpoint handoffs, and export.

Give your coding agent the skill and dataset location. Follow the environment checks, validate a sample, and test training and restart before a longer run. Evaluate quality on held-out episodes: a successful short run verifies execution, not convergence.

#9594. Sellfy Review 2022: How Good Is This Ecommerce Platform?

 


Are you searching for an ecomerce platform to help you build an online store and sell products?

In this Sellfy review, we'll talk about how this eCommerce platform can let you sell digital products while keeping full control of your marketing.

And the best part? Starting your business can be done in just five minutes.

Let us then talk about the Sellfy platform and all the benefits it can bring to your business.

What is Sellfy?

Sellfy is an eCommerce solution that allows digital content creators, including writers, illustrators, designers, musicians, and filmmakers, to sell their products online. Sellfy provides a customizable storefront where users can display their digital products and embed "Buy Now" buttons on their website or blog. Sellfy product pages enable users to showcase their products from different angles with multiple images and previews from Soundcloud, Vimeo, and YouTube. Files of up to 2GB can be uploaded to Sellfy, and the company offers unlimited bandwidth and secure file storage. Users can also embed their entire store or individual project widgets in their site, with the ability to preview how widgets will appear before they are displayed.

Features

Sellfy includes:

Online Store

Sellfy is a powerful e-commerce platform that helps you personalize your online storefront. You can add your logo, change colors, revise navigation, and edit the layout of your store. Sellfy also allows you to create a full shopping cart so customers can purchase multiple items. And Sellfy gives you the ability to set your language or let customers see a translated version of your store based on their location.

Sellfy gives you the option to host your store directly on its platform, add a custom domain to your store, and use it as an embedded storefront on your website. Sellfy also optimizes its store offerings for mobile devices, allowing for a seamless checkout experience.

Product hosting

Sellfy allows creators to host all their products and sell all of their digital products on one platform. Sellfy also does not place storage limits on your store but recommends that files be no larger than 5GB. Creators can sell both standard and subscription-based products in any file format that is supported by the online marketplace. Customers can purchase products instantly after making a purchase – there is no waiting period.

You can organize your store by creating your product categories, sorting by any characteristic you choose. Your title, description, and the image will be included on each product page. In this way, customers can immediately evaluate all of your products. You can offer different pricing options for all of your products, including "pay what you want," in which the price is entirely up to the customer. This option allows you to give customers control over the cost of individual items (without a minimum price) or to set pricing minimums—a good option if you're in a competitive market or when you have higher-end products. You can also offer set prices per product as well as free products to help build your store's popularity.

Sellfy is ideal for selling digital content, such as ebooks. But it does not allow you to copyrighted material (that you don't have rights to distribute).

Embed options

Sellfy offers several ways to share your store, enabling you to promote your business on different platforms. Sellfy lets you integrate it with your existing website using "buy now" buttons, embed your entire storefront, or embed certain products so you can reach more people. Sellfy also enables you to connect with your Facebook page and YouTube channel, maximizing your visibility.

Payments and security

Sellfy is a simple online platform that allows customers to buy your products directly through your store. Sellfy has two payment processing options: PayPal and Stripe. You will receive instant payments with both of these processors, and your customer data is protected by Sellfy's secure (PCI-compliant) payment security measures. In addition to payment security, Sellfy provides anti-fraud tools to help protect your products including PDF stamping, unique download links, and limited download attempts.


Marketing and analytics tools

The Sellfy platform includes marketing and analytics tools to help you manage your online store. You can send email product updates and collect newsletter subscribers through the platform. With Sellfy, you can also offer discount codes and product upsells, as well as create and track Facebook and Twitter ads for your store. The software's analytics dashboard will help you track your best-performing products, generated revenue, traffic channels, top locations, and overall store performance.

Integrations

To expand functionality and make your e-commerce store run more efficiently, Sellfy offers several integrations. Google Analytics and Webhooks, as well as integrations with Patreon and Facebook Live Chat, are just a few of the options available. Sellfy allows you to connect to Zapier, which gives you access to hundreds of third-party apps, including tools like Mailchimp, Trello, Salesforce, and more.

Sellfy Review: Pros and Cons

Sellfy has its benefits and downsides, but fortunately, the pros outweigh the cons.

Pros

  • You can sell your products on a single storefront, even if you are selling multiple product types.

Cons

#9593. How long does pie last in the fridge? : Because we're all wondering what to do with our apple and pumpkin pies.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions. Today: How long does pie last in the fridge?

The season of plentiful pies is upon us. When preparing several pies for a holiday meal, you may be wondering about the imminent leftovers. Should apple pie be stored differently than pumpkin pie? David from our Baker’s Hotline is here with his expert advice to help.

“Baked apple or other fruit pies can be kept covered, at room temperature, for one to two days. After that, they’ll keep in the fridge for one to two more days,” David advises. A 15-minute reheat in a 350°F oven can help revive some of that freshly baked flavor. Tent the pie with foil so it doesn’t brown further.

Interested in prepping ahead? David says that storing an assembled, ready-to-bake apple pie is a bad idea; the fruity filling will release moisture, which will make your crust soggy. Instead, roll out your pie crusts and prep your apples, but keep them separate. And wait to add the sugar and spices to the apples until you’re ready to bake the pie. This way, you can pour off any liquid that’s accumulated from the fruit without draining off your thickener, sugar, and spices.

Sliced apples turn brown, so you don’t want to keep your prepared apples in the fridge very long before baking. Aim for under 24 hours, but a squeeze of lemon juice could help them last another day or so.

And if you want to use your freezer to prep ahead, here’s how to freeze and bake fruit pies.

David advises, “Baked pumpkin pie or other pies containing eggs and/or dairy such as pecan pie, custard pie, or chiffon pie should be stored refrigerated; they’ll keep in the fridge for three to four days. I like to transfer the pie to a shallow, lidded storage container, but plastic wrap or a storage top can be used as well.”

As with apple, if you’re making your pumpkin (and other custard) pie ahead, it’s best to keep filling and crust separate. Pumpkin pie filling can be made ahead; it’ll keep, refrigerated, overnight. In fact, that's actually what we recommend doing; the custard develops incredible flavor and aroma as it sits.

If you can, serve pies the day they were made instead of refrigerating them.

Reheat refrigerated pies in a 350°F oven for about 15 minutes prior to serving.

Apple and other fruit pies will last at room temperature for up to two days, then in the fridge for two more.

Pumpkin, custard, or other egg/dairy-based pies can be stored in the fridge for up to four days.

If you’re making the crust and the filling ahead, keep them separated until it’s time to bake your pie.

#9591. How to Build a B2B Lead Generation Strategy Across Multiple Channels

Content Creator & PR Consultant- Contributes to GoDaddy, Social Samosa, The Chakkar, Hackernoon & so on.

Content Creator & PR Consultant- Contributes to GoDaddy, Social Samosa, The Chakkar, Hackernoon & so on.

Content Creator & PR Consultant- Contributes to GoDaddy, Social Samosa, The Chakkar, Hackernoon & so on.

Amongst the most difficult tasks ever performed by a working professional is getting good-quality, actionable sales leads. Ask any CEO, entrepreneur, marketing head or salesperson, and they will tell you the same thing. It is like prospecting for water in a desert or oil on a mountaintop. According to a recent survey, 47% of B2B marketers feel they lack efficient lead generation and nurturing processes (The Content Marketing Institute, 2025).

As a young twenty-something sales manager in a leading timeshare company, even getting close to my monthly sales target was akin to a nightmare. The lead generation support from the company was never enough to create a pipeline big enough to make one even think of ever achieving or surpassing the monthly target. Add to that the fact that my team of sales executives was quick to promise results, but hopelessly negligent in coming anywhere near them.

It was largely on account of sheer grinding that one stayed afloat and even managed to occasionally crack a super deal or two. But there were a few colleagues who seemed to achieve their targets with consummate ease and made me wonder- what magic did they possess that I did not?

Through my career in sales and marketing before I made the switch to PR and communications, the process of generating actionable leads has both frustrated and fascinated me. Today, as a communications and PR solopreneur, I find that generating actionable leads is as fascinating and challenging as ever.

I have condensed my learning about the lead generation and sales process over the years into six essential parts:

You may not have the budget for a sustained advertising campaign, but you can look at sending out emails to the right segment of potential customers and obtain a not insignificant number of leads which you can then try and convert.

When I had started out, one would actually send out beautifully designed mailers by post, often deploying a franking machine to stamp them with the right value of postage. Mailers even then were quite an efficient direct marketing technique with good ROI, as they are now.

Once you have a few initial sales closures under your belt, you need to ensure that you provide your new customers with exemplary service so that they are happy to have dealt with you. This will make them refer you to other potential customers. A recommendation from an existing client shortens the sales cycle considerably. What’s more, if your existing clientele or customers are pleased with your services or products, they will remain your clients for longer or become repeat customers. According to Nielsen’s 2021 global Trust in Advertising study, 88% of respondents held the view that they trusted recommendations from people they knew.

This type of networking is what puts you on the fast track to success. When I struck out on my own as a PR and content consultant, it was the goodwill of my old clients that quickly enabled me to establish myself.

When I started my career in the early nineties, traditional advertisements in the shape of print and magazine ads, TV commercials, outdoor hoardings, kiosks hung from electric poles, and bus panels were an expensive and highly effective way of attracting customers. The advent of the digital age may have altered the focus of advertising, but traditional forms of it remain valid and relevant, especially for big brands. In the era of very targeted digital advertising, traditional advertising remains much in demand for spreading brand awareness across a wide geography.

Somewhere along my career, I pivoted to Public Relations and worked for some of the leading PR names in the industry. Now PR was something that established brands, or brands that wanted to acquire heft, went for.

Getting the media of the land to cover a brand, not because they were paid to do so, but because their news story warranted it, added credibility to a brand that no amount of advertising could. Adding PR to a company’s outreach is definitely a step up and can lead to the generation of a huge amount of business if done in the right manner.

The digital marketing age is truly upon us and has levelled the playing field for businesses across scale. No longer is one constrained by the lack of resources to mount an expensive outreach exercise or the absence of a well-established network of clients and the people referred by them.

Instead, it is data-driven, targeted and inbound in its orientation. Of course, it has a healthy outbound component as well in the shape of paid social media ads, other display ads and email campaigns. What's more, it often costs a fraction of what a traditional campaign would and delivers far more quantifiable results.

As far as inbound marketing is concerned, content marketing, including thought leadership, is an integral part of it. We live in the age of rapid dissemination of knowledge and information through social media, and having had a facility for language helped me reach out to potential clients through my blog and social media posts in a manner that was both delightful and surprising to me.

Quality content that offers direction or any kind of helpful advice generates trust in an individual or brand, which ultimately may result in leads. This is especially true now, when consumers of products and services carry out research more often than not with the help of AI. Research carried out by Gartner in 2026 discovered that 45% of B2B buyers had made use of AI as part of their purchase process recently.

There is an old analogy from the world of boxing where your success depends not so much on how often you can hit your opponents, but on your ability to absorb the knocks your opponent delivers and still fight on to win. Your sales successes might pump you up and fill you with enthusiasm, but your periods of drought should not let you throw in the towel. You have to persist and hang in there. More startups have closed just short of turning the corner because the people in charge couldn’t hang in there a little longer.

You may, for instance, get in touch with a hundred prospects and have no luck in converting any of them, and on the other hand land two clients after contacting just twenty. The right timing is often the difference between success and failure here. That is why you have to be persistent with your follow-up. Who knows, the next time you follow up with a prospect, they may just have been allocated the budget to sign up with you. While this kind of resilience is very important for all businesses, it is particularly so for solopreneurs. You need to figure out which approaches work and which don’t, even while ensuring that a dry spell does not crush your spirit.

Towards the end, I would like to submit that if there continues to be an air of mystery to the process of getting actionable leads, it is because it depends on a lot of variables that you have no control over. It is a lot like flying-you may have the best weather forecast available to you, which predicts favourable tailwinds, and yet run into severe headwinds. Your skill lies in still making a successful landing. The more experience you get under your belt, the better you become at it, but you still have to respect the elements. Above all, you need to have the staying power to weather the troughs and capitalise on the highs.

Content Distribution Matters as Much as Content Creation

#9589. ToyBlocks: A controlled world for robot learning and evaluation

💻 Code | 📊 Data | 🤖 Models | 📖 Documentation

Robots are learning to fold laundry, sort parts, and handle unfamiliar objects. But those demonstrations are often rather narrow and don't explain what a robot has learned or why it fails.

To study a complex system, scientists often begin with a small, controlled environment, such as a petri dish or terrarium, where they can vary conditions and observe the effects. Robotics needs environments that make this kind of investigation possible—researchers should be able to change the training data or model design, repeat a test, and trace the cause of a failure.

Today we're introducing a framework for creating these environments; we call them FoundationWorlds. Each pairs a controlled, simulated world targeted at studying robotics in a specific environment with tools for automatically generating tasks and training demonstrations, as well as metrics for measuring a robot's behavior over time. Together, they provide a setting for studying questions such as how models improve as more training data becomes available, and how to best combine high-level reasoning with precise physical control.

Our first foundation world is ToyBlocks: an open simulation framework built around a robot arm and blocks on a tabletop. The setting is deliberately simple, but the robot must still reason about how the blocks interact and how to arrange them while pushing, flipping, and stacking.

ToyBlocks automatically generates demonstrations, which are recordings of a robot completing tasks in simulation, without requiring time-consuming teleoperation, in which a person remotely controls the robot. Researchers can easily vary these training experiences. For example, a team could generate more pushing or flipping demonstrations, then evaluate performance on tasks kept out of training.

Starting with ToyBlocks as our first FoundationWorld, we aim to extend the approach to increasingly complex environments.

Building on our earlier work in open robot learning, including MolmoAct 2, MolmoBot, and MolmoSpaces, ToyBlocks gives researchers a way to study robotics questions in a deliberately constrained domain.

As a FoundationWorld, ToyBlocks is designed around four requirements: (1) realistic physics and appearance, (2) automatic generation of tasks and demonstrations at scale, (3) challenges that combine reasoning with dexterity, and (4) broad coverage of the tasks possible within a domain.

Open-ended domains require modeling a wide range of objects and interactions, making it infeasible to fulfill all these requirements. ToyBlocks’ narrow scope, on the other hand, makes it possible to fulfill them all.

Within ToyBlocks' smaller setting, researchers can work toward investigating how a robot can learn to perform any reasonable task while being confident that the simulated arm and blocks behave very similarly to their physical counterparts.

A physical robot gripper above wooden blocks in the ToyBlocks setup.

ToyBlocks is not just about picking and stacking blocks: pictures and letters on the blocks' faces allow for searching, sorting, and arranging tasks. A robot may need to turn a block to see a hidden face before deciding where it belongs. Domain randomization – varying block size, table height, and other physical properties from scene to scene – tests how well models generalize as the geometry changes.

ToyBlocks automatically generates skills (behaviors for short tasks) and task demonstrations that can be used to train models or adapt previously trained models through additional training (fine-tuning). High-level reasoning models decide what to do; low-level action models control the robot’s movements. The framework can also be used to easily design experiments and validate hypotheses.

ToyBlocks uses reinforcement learning (RL) and motion planning, which computes how the robot should move, to generate skills for short-horizon tasks, which involve brief sequences of actions. Skill training takes place in Isaac Lab, Nvidia's open-source framework for robot learning in simulation. Through trial and error, these policies – models that choose the robot’s actions – learn non-prehensile skills such as pushing a block across the table or flipping it onto another face without picking it up. Skill generation can draw on privileged information – values the simulator can supply directly but a real robot cannot, such as a block's exact position and orientation – instead of estimating it from camera images. This enables the automatic generation of skills that would require teleoperation in the real world.

To generate demonstration data, a task-and-motion planner (TAMP) automatically selects and sequences the skills needed to solve a task and plans the robot’s movements between them. Running each plan in simulation produces a dataset of recorded demonstrations along with labels describing which task or skill the robot performs. ToyBlocks scales data generation through generating and executing hundreds of such plans in parallel on a single graphics processing unit (GPU), reaching up to 24 times real-time performance.

Acting from sensor observations adds a perception problem: a model has to estimate a block’s pose – its position and orientation – which the simulator could supply directly. To reflect real-world conditions, ToyBlocks trains models that map raw sensor observations to actions.

Execution of Molmo 2 (a high-level model) and ManiFlow (a low-level model) trained in ToyBlocks. Molmo 2 selects skills such as rotation and flipping, indicating the relevant block via a pointing interface, while ManiFlow controls the simulated arm to execute the commanded skills.

ToyBlocks' controllable data generator lets users create training mixtures that emphasize particular skills or fill gaps in existing datasets. Researchers can study how much data a model needs and which experiences help it generalize to unseen tasks. For example, they could test whether adding rotation and pick-and-place demonstrations improves flipping, or vary the balance of examples inside and outside a defined workspace region—evaluating their choices on tasks kept out of training. Importantly, evaluation of trained models generates metrics beyond success rates; it provides information such as execution speeds, forces exerted on objects, and task progress measured via the same specifications used by the planning module.

A webpage interface lets users connect Claude – or another frontier model – and use natural language to instruct the robot or try tasks, offering a way to explore how a model plans and acts without needing robotics expertise.

The evaluations below use ToyBlocks to study how training data and methods affect performance, spatial reasoning, generalization to new letters and block appearances, multi-step planning, transfer to physical robots, and frontier models that act through tools. Users can easily design their own tasks and measures to investigate other questions—for example, whether a model performs better when it selects objects by pointing or by issuing text commands such as "pick the yellow block."

Low-level action models, such as vision-language-action models (VLAs), map language instructions and visual observations to robot actions.

The premise of VLAs is that, by pretraining on large-scale datasets, they can rapidly generalize to different scenarios or a specific workspace. However, evidence on how well these action models generalize remains conflicting. Some studies report that these action models are brittle to changes in inputs, such as different object layouts and lighting, whereas others show that VLAs generalize well. We argue that these studies often rely on real-world datasets with limited flexibility in spatial variations. ToyBlocks enables us to test how well action models generalize in a simple, easily reproducible setting with meaningful task-space diversity.

We design generalization tests that vary the skill sequences needed to complete an instruction, the letters or colors on the blocks, and the number of blocks in a scene. A stacking study can withhold four-block stacks from training, then test whether a model can combine familiar movements to build them. Workspace studies distinguish performance at new positions within a training region from performance beyond its boundaries, where the model has to extrapolate. We illustrate the study setup and findings below.

We consider four tasks: Stack, Unstack, Flip, and Rotate. For these tasks, we study interpolation (new configurations within the training range) and extrapolation (configurations beyond that range). For example, we evaluate generalization by training on scenarios where objects spawn only in the left region (green) and testing on the right region (orange), or by training on stack heights of 2 and 5 blocks and testing on heights 3 and 4.

Spatial generalization studies for VLA models (results based on ManiFlow, π0.5, and MolmoAct 2). Despite large-scale pretraining, these popular action models generalize poorly in the initial results. We improve generalization and analyze the contribution of each technique. The chart’s LoRA label stands for low-rank adaptation, a method for fine-tuning a model with a small set of trainable weight updates. We believe action model generalization remains far from solved; ToyBlocks provides a valuable testbed for systematically exploring generalization techniques.

Long-horizon tasks, which require many steps, allow us to measure how well models can plan a sequence of actions to solve them. Our framework enables us to create such long-horizon tasks, and create oracles – reference components that provide correct plans or actions – at both the high and low levels. This allows us to isolate whether the high-level planning or low-level execution failed when a model fails at a task. An example long-horizon task might be to spell “Ai2” with a block stack; because the letters may not be immediately visible, the agent must first choose actions that reveal information, and then plan and execute a sequence of actions to build the stack.

We evaluate hierarchical models with explicit high-level planning and low-level execution models. In this instance, we choose Molmo 2, a vision-language model (VLM), as the high-level planner, and ManiFlow as the low-level policy. Molmo 2 chooses the skill to execute and the block to execute it on, while the low-level model executes the instruction. We train low-level models such as ManiFlow to pause after completing the execution and query the high-level model for the next instruction. We evaluate the model’s planning abilities on three scenarios of increasing difficulty. The easiest scenario initializes with each character upright and facing the camera. The medium scenario has characters that may not be upright, and the hardest scenario contains characters that are not visible at the start of the episode.

Success rates on three-letter block-spelling tasks using Molmo 2 as the high-level reasoning model and either ManiFlow or a motion planner for low-level manipulation. An example task is “Stack Ai2”. Molmo 2 and ManiFlow are trained on ToyBlocks and evaluated across three difficulty settings and two generalization conditions.

Our experiments with agentic systems test how frontier models plan and act through tool calls. We study three settings using Claude Opus 5.5. In the search-and-spell setting, we expose ToyBlocks skills through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a standard for connecting AI applications to tools. The agent sees the scene through camera images, calls skills such as pick, flip, or rotate by pointing at a pixel, and decides when to search, build, or declare the task complete or impossible. The same MCP tools can execute either the scripted skills that generate ToyBlocks demonstrations (motion-planned pick and place, plus RL-based rotate and flip) or learned ManiFlow skills. ToyBlocks includes the framework behind these experiments, which also powers the natural-language web interface described earlier.

A frontier model (Claude Fable 5.1) controls a robot in a ToyBlocks world to search for and stack blocks into a tower spelling “Ai2.” During the episode, the agent muses, “I need to figure out whether pick-and-place naturally straightens orientation or if I need to correct it manually… I have 63 calls left, plenty to run a controlled test” (0:06). The agent later hypothesizes: “…maybe the gripper’s yaw is radial—pointing from the robot base toward the block” (0:15) and eventually confirms this hypothesis (0:26) before constructing the three-block tower, but the ‘A’ is sideways (1:11). Surprisingly, current frontier models often make similar perceptual errors (see the next figure), despite their impressive planning, spatial reasoning, and search capabilities.

For classical planning, the agent (our system using Claude Opus 5.5 to plan and choose actions) solves all 30 of a group of block-stacking tasks similar to ones that frontier models struggled with a few years ago, using text descriptions. It also solves 30 out of 30 while repeatedly observing camera images and choosing its next action in a closed loop.

In the search-and-spell setting, the agent had to generate stacks spelling out three-letter words. It had to find the blocks with the corresponding letters among up to eight blocks in the scene. Importantly, 50% of the scenes did not have blocks with all the required letters, rendering the task infeasible. In this case, we required the agent to state that the task is infeasible. We found that in this experiment, the agent was able to successfully solve or correctly declare infeasible 63% of the tasks. Errors were mostly caused by the agent confusing letters with look-alike letters (13%) or choosing an incorrect orientation for a letter in a stack (15%).

Our results also show that the agent was able to solve the task more efficiently when the blocks had semantic regularities, or patterns, taking advantage of such patterns to reason about occluded faces. For instance, in most of the infeasible scenes, when the blocks had no patterns, the agent correctly looked at all the blocks’ faces before declaring infeasibility, whereas it was able to declare infeasibility significantly faster when the blocks had semantic patterns.

Our third experimental setting asks whether an agent can learn how its skills behave, using experiments as a scientist would. When a skill behaves unexpectedly, the agent forms a hypothesis, designs a small test, and revises its understanding from the result. We expand on this idea by having an agent run its own experiments and write its own skill descriptions based on what it finds. These learned descriptions raise success rates from 24% with the default descriptions to 63%, outperforming the 36% achieved with descriptions written by a human expert.

Share of letter-block faces the agent had exposed by the end of each “search and spell” episode (bars averaged over 20 episodes; one marker per episode, styled by outcome). In a feasible task every letter of the three-letter target word is present; in an infeasible task, one letter is missing and the agent should say so. Each patterned block carries uppercase and lowercase instances of a letter, plus images that begin with the letter (e.g., A-block: apple, ant, A, 1, airplane, a); an unpatterned block’s six faces are randomized and unrelated. Correct: the tower spelled the word, or for infeasible tasks, the agent correctly declared the task impossible. Letter rotated or look-alike: the agent built the tower, but a letter was turned or a look-alike substituted, including five infeasible tasks declared solved with a look-alike in the missing letter’s place. Block fell out of reach; reported: a needed block was pushed out of the arm’s reach, so the agent reported that its task had become impossible. No report: the agent used up its motor-skill budget and stopped without claiming either outcome. With patterned blocks, the agent finishes having seen fewer faces, because it can infer what hidden faces must depict rather than checking every one.

Action-conditioned world models are trained to predict how a scene changes in response to a robot’s actions. Using them as an alternative to model-based simulators for training and evaluating robot policies is an active area of research. How well they serve this purpose depends on how accurately they predict physical interactions, which is hard to measure without knowing the true state of the scene. ToyBlocks provides this ground truth – the actual simulated scene state – enabling highly controlled tests of how recently developed world models perform in low-level object manipulation. Here, the arm’s end effector is its gripper.

Specifically, we tested whether action-conditioned world models are capable of predicting the motions of blocks or the outcomes of skill executions after being trained on example executions. To do so, we chose four different skills (pick-and-place, flip, rotate, and a mixed task) and generated 900 trajectories – sequences of robot states and actions over time – for each skill. 50% of these trajectories were successful demonstrations of the skill, and 50% were unsuccessful because of small changes to spatial configurations. With equal numbers of successful and unsuccessful executions, a model that always predicts success would be correct only half the time. The models were fine-tuned on these demonstrations and then tested on their ability to predict the outcome of action sequences of the same skills.

We find that Wan 2.2 predicts block motion and task outcomes most accurately. Astra tracks the gripper well but struggles to simulate contact. LeWM is fast and more accurate over short interaction segments, though it drifts over full trajectories. In additional experiments, we also showed that models that score higher on pose and success prediction also produce better training data: adding 100 model-generated trajectories (rollouts) from the best video-generation model raises a policy’s success in an unseen region from 19% to 78%.

We tested three types of models: a video prediction model with 5 billion parameters (Wan 2.2), an agentic model that created its own physics simulator tuned to match the demonstration data (Astra), and a latent world model (LeWM). During testing, each trained model has to predict future images, simulator states, or latent states (learned internal representations), respectively, based on an initial image and a sequence of actions. For full trajectories, models use the initial image as the only observed image, along with the action sequence. For short interaction segments – a single pick, place, flip, or rotate – models start from the real image immediately before that interaction. Full trajectories show how errors accumulate over long horizons, while interaction segments isolate a single interaction, such as the gripper making contact with a block, and show how well the model predicts it. To compare models fairly, we probe each model’s predictions, reading out where it expects the blocks and gripper to be at different points in the trajectory and whether it expects the task to succeed at the end.

Sim-to-real evaluations test policies trained in simulation on physical robots performing block manipulation tasks. By comparing simulation and real-world execution, we assess whether behaviors and failure patterns observed in simulation provide meaningful indications of real-world performance. For example, researchers can evaluate individual skills and their composition in longer-horizon tasks to identify where failures arise and whether these patterns carry over to physical deployments.

We test whether the models trained entirely on ToyBlocks simulation datasets can be deployed in the real world zero-shot, without training on real-world examples. We evaluate ManiFlow and each low-level skill (pick, place, flip, and rotate) individually. We test whether the hierarchical system (Molmo 2 + ManiFlow) can complete long-horizon three-block spelling tasks requiring sequences of these actions. Real-world experiments use a Franka FR3 arm with a Robotiq gripper across thirty scene configurations. Each scene contains 4–10 blocks seen during training. An episode is successful only if the relevant blocks are moved to target poses without collisions. If the operator intervenes to stop the robot due to an unsafe motion during an episode, it is marked as a failure.

ManiFlow’s atomic-skill success rates were similar in simulation and the real world (80.0% and 81.1%). The hierarchical Molmo 2 + ManiFlow system succeeded in 55.5% of simulated episodes (111/200) and 50.0% of real-world episodes (15/30); further trials are needed to establish statistical confidence across tasks.

Success rates of the ManiFlow low-level model and the hierarchical Molmo 2–ManiFlow system in simulation and the real world. For ManiFlow, the total count represents individual skill executions (pick, place, flip, and rotate), whereas for Molmo 2–ManiFlow, it represents block-spelling task episodes. The Molmo 2–ManiFlow evaluations use the easiest scene configuration defined in the simulation evaluation, with block characters visible and upright.

Side-by-side real-world and simulated block-stacking executions using the same high-level planner. Pink rings mark the planner’s target point for each skill. The scenes use different block labels, and simulation playback is retimed to align grasps and releases with the real robot.

To transfer Molmo 2 and ManiFlow – both trained exclusively on ToyBlocks data – to a physical robot, we address the differences between simulation and reality in three stages.

Before data generation, we perform system identification by tuning simulated robot parameters, including joint friction and armature (the motor and gearbox inertia reflected at the joint), to match real-robot trajectories. During data generation, we randomize physical properties (object size, friction, and table height) and visual properties (lighting, backgrounds, materials, and camera parameters). At inference time, observations are captured using a front-facing ZED camera and a wrist-mounted ZED Mini. For policies that use depth images, we generate clean depth maps, which estimate distance at each pixel, from paired red-green-blue (RGB) camera images using FastFoundationStereo, rather than relying on noisy depth sensor measurements.

The physical ToyBlocks setup: a robot arm, wooden blocks, and a camera.

ToyBlocks connects data generation, training, and evaluation in one controlled setting, so researchers can investigate how robots learn over time and test how changes to a model or its training data affect robot behavior. We’re releasing simulation assets, procedural task and demonstration generators, automatically generated demonstrations, two trained models showcasing what the framework can do (one based on Molmo 2 and one based on ManiFlow), training code, and evaluation code and validation sets. This allows other teams to build their own training mixtures and investigate failure modes beyond those covered in our initial experiments.

Our initial data release is a proof point with 85,336 long-horizon demonstrations, each comprising about 6–12 skill demonstrations, depending on the set. The initial datasets cover nearly 1,600 hours of robot execution data and 144 million frames. In a few weeks, we're targeting a second release with a larger-scale dataset, more skills, and more comprehensive benchmarking. We’ll also add fully integrated RL training capability that is not contained in the current package.

Other directions for ToyBlocks include bimanual (two-arm) manipulation and dexterous robot hands, equipped with force and touch sensors for studying motion and tasks that involve frequent physical contact. We're also exploring play with unstructured piles of blocks as a way to collect data and study how new behaviors and tasks might emerge through interaction.

Future direction: RL-based pile manipulation.

Future direction: bimanual block manipulation.

With ToyBlocks, we want to advance the science of robot learning toward a future where robots can reliably apply what they've learned to unfamiliar tasks and environments. We encourage the research community to explore ToyBlocks for their own investigations and even as a basis to build their own FoundationWorlds.

#9588. ProWritingAid VS Grammarly: Which Grammar Checker is Better in (2022) ?

Grammarly is a tool that checks for grammatical errors, spelling, and punctuation.it gives you comprehensive feedback on your writing. You can use this tool to proofread and edit articles, blog posts, emails, etc.

Grammarly also detects all types of mistakes, including sentence structure issues and misused words. It also gives you suggestions on style changes, punctuation, spelling, and grammar all are in real-time. The free version covers the basics like identifying grammar and spelling mistakes

whereas the Premium version offers a lot more functionality, it detects plagiarism in your content, suggests word choice, or adds fluency to it.

ProWritingAid is a style and grammar checker for content creators and writers. It helps to optimize word choice, punctuation errors, and common grammar mistakes, providing detailed reports to help you improve your writing.

ProWritingAid can be used as an add-on to WordPress, Gmail, and Google Docs. The software also offers helpful articles, videos, quizzes, and explanations to help improve your writing.

Here are some key features of ProWriting Aid:

Grammarly and ProWritingAid are well-known grammar-checking software. However, if you're like most people who can't decide which to use, here are some different points that may be helpful in your decision.

As both writing assistants are great in their own way, you need to choose the one that suits you best.

Both ProWritingAid and Grammarly are awesome writing tools, without a doubt. but as per my experience, Grammarly is a winner here because Grammarly helps you to review and edit your content. Grammarly highlights all the mistakes in your writing within seconds of copying and pasting the content into Grammarly’s editor or using the software’s native feature in other text editors.

Not only does it identify tiny grammatical and spelling errors, it tells you when you overlook punctuations where they are needed. And, beyond its plagiarism-checking capabilities, Grammarly helps you proofread your content. Even better, the software offers a free plan that gives you access to some of its features.

Sounds like you're biased for Grammarly. Not really that informative if you're already leaning towards one to begin with. Still, it was an interesting read. Tell me, do you use Grammarly with your day-to-day writing/blogging?

I use the paid versions of both Grammarly and Pro Writing Aid. Both of them have issues:- Grammarly IS more focused on nonfiction than fiction. If you're writing fiction, you may find Grammarly's insistence on "Conciseness" annoying. They seem to want to take the soul out of your writing, which is fine for a corporate report or technical manual, but not for your Great American Novel.- Grammarly pushes features on users that are not ready for prime time. It doesn't matter that you never agreed to be a beta tester for them; you get to do it anyway.- Pro Writing Aid actually counts the occurrences of words in your document and tells you when a word has been overused compared to published literature. Grammarly, on the other hand, seems hell-bent to remove certain words that it has deemed overused from the language, whether or not they're actually overused in your document.- Grammarly's Clarity function is simply horrible. It mangles sentences and changes their meaning. Sometimes the result of its suggestion is unintelligible garbage.- Grammarly allows you to turn off some checks, but not all of them. Unfortunately, the ones you cannot turn off are some of the most irritating (such as that horrible "Clarity"). On the other hand, Pro Writing Aid lets you choose which checks you use.- Pro Writing Aid has a mediocre command of American English (it's a British product). The app insists on rules of grammar and spelling that are outright wrong, per Merriam-Webster, the Chicago Manual of Style, and modern usage as shown by Google Books Ngram. At one point, Pro Writing Aid insisted that American English did not include the words "holiday" and "autumn," that "vacation" and "fall" must be used instead.- Pro Writing Aid's rules for commas are 100 percent consistent with the way I learned them in high school--50 years ago! They do not reflect modern usage. Grammarly is much better at this.- Pro Writing Aid seems to waste their limited resources on tweaking their UI. Their UI most definitely could use improvement, but these changes are not great improvements; they only serve to confuse users. Their resources would be better spent fixing the many functional problems in their app.- Some of Pro Writing Aid's checks are completely useless, as they do not take context into consideration. For example, an ordinary word would not be capitalized as part of a narrative, but would be as part of a title (for example, "professor." But if you capitalize correctly for context, Pro Writing Aid dings you for "Inconsistent capitalization." Similar issues exist with hyphenation consistency check.Each of these applications has its strengths as well as considerable weaknesses. I will say that both of them are light-years better than the execrable grammar checker in Microsoft Word, but that's damning with faint praise.

#9587. What Would It Take to Prove That an AI Is Conscious?

Adventuring philosopher, Pompous pontificator, Writer, Biohacker, Tantric husband, Raconteur & Smart Drug Dealer

Adventuring philosopher, Pompous pontificator, Writer, Biohacker, Tantric husband, Raconteur & Smart Drug Dealer

Adventuring philosopher, Pompous pontificator, Writer, Biohacker, Tantric husband, Raconteur & Smart Drug Dealer

A revolution is upon us, and whenever a revolution occurs, a new aristocracy is minted. The new aristocracy will be an aristocracy of intelligence.

Intelligence has always been the human resource--from the first flight on Kittyhawk beach to footsteps on the moon; from humans living in a state of stark barbarism and despotism for millennia to universal human rights so close to our grasp today--it was intelligence that got from there to here.

In the velocopdic era of modernity, we have built digital gods that would make our ancestors tremble; with omniscience, omnipresence, and omnipotence that would rival nearly any mythological deity. I'm talking about artificial intelligence, of course.Thanks to AI, the resource our species needs to thrive is now seemingly limitless. With intelligence unlimited, we can build an economy of abundance, make governments sane again (if we need them at all), cure disease, and make death an option instead of the inevitability. With intelligence inexhaustible, our descendants can sprinkle the cosmos with human brilliance. And I, for one, plan to one day swing dance with my wife on the peak of Olympus Mons!

**But is that all direly naive? \ Will AI instead take all our jobs? And usher us into a cyberpunk dystopia that the greatest science fiction writers of the past century could scarcely fathom, chain-smoking at 2 AM on their seventh cup of coffee? With the invention of general artificial intelligence within sight, with this revolution, have we instead summoned the demon, opened the last Pandora's box, and birthed "the Borg?"

I think that comes down to the question we've all asked: is AI conscious?

Many are now asking a very big question: Is AI conscious?

Recently, I watched an excellent documentary, AM I? Which approaches this question with the trepidation it deserves...

The Silicon Valley types grappling with this question seem to view it through a narrow scientific materialist lens. I suspect this bias has made them ignore the very consciousness science that would ultimately answer the question: Is AI conscious or sentient in the same way that other higher mammals and we are?

If you're a spiritual person of faith, you're nodding along, saying: "Of course, human consciousness hacks reality!" But if you're a skeptical materialist, I need to present evidence for my extraordinary claim.

This is the most scientifically proven fact by the highest quality of science. Hundreds of thousands of gold-standard clinical trials, encompassing many millions of human participants, have demonstrated the power of belief in the ever-present placebo effect. The placebo effect can be partially explained by neuropeptides communicating with the epigenome, but there remain examples of the placebo effect doing things that cannot be explained. Some mind-blowing examples from "You Are the Placebo" by Dr. Joe Dispenza...

In a 2002 trial of 180 patients (that's statistically significant), some received sham placebo surgery, and amazingly their knees healed themselves, their pain went away and the patients could walk again, neither of the two groups who actually had the surgery improved any more than the patients who received the placebo surgery—and this held true even after two years.

Fake heart surgery is similarly effective, 67 percent of the patients who had received the actual surgery felt less pain and needed less medication, while 83 percent of those who had received the sham surgery enjoyed the same level of improvement. The placebo surgery had actually worked better than the real surgery!

A Harvard study of elderly men who were placed in an environment for several days that was meticulously and convincingly designed to feel like it was from 22 years earlier and the men's biological aging markers when measured showed a positive regression towards a more youthful state. They felt and acted younger and amazingly various symptoms of aging disappeared in just a few days.

A wheelchair-bound woman suffering from crippling multiple sclerosis who healed herself and reversed her condition just by the power of meditation. People who died of cancer that upon autopsy didn't actually have cancer.

The awesome power of the placebo is the most well-established phenomenon in science. In your own experience (or that of those close to you), you can probably think of examples of the placebo effect working. The placebo effect is so common that over 160,000 published clinical trials mention it prominently; it's a universal factor in our health.

Science seeks truth, but does not claim to have captured it. Science is the endeavor of asymptotically approaching the truth of reality. The veridical asymptote that has stood the test of thousands of clinical trials is that belief hacks physical reality. Jesus turned water into wine, and if I put water in a bottle of Grey Goose vodka and convince you it's vodka, you'll likely get drunk because human consciousness hacks physical reality. But the placebo effect is not the only example; there are many others...

While the standard observer effect in physics often refers to the mechanical interaction of a measurement device, Dean Radin’s studies (replicated over decades) involve human intention.

There's a particularly good documentary that details the replication of the Double-Slit Experiment, The Simulation Hypothesis by Kent Forbes.

These experiments, often associated with Dean Radin and Dick Bierman, suggest that consciousness "leaks" from the future into the present.

This connects to Daryl Bem’s "Feeling the future" experiments, where they discovered "time traveling porn," yes. I'll let Grok describe it...

Skin conductance, heart rate, pupil dilation, or EEG changes appear before randomly selected emotional (vs. calm) images or stimuli. Meta-analyses of presentiment-style work have reported small effects; Bem’s 2011 JPSP package of nine experiments claimed retroactive influence.

I actually used this as the basis for the "time hacking" mechanic of a science fiction novel I wrote--I'll tell you more about that later.

This project utilizes a global network of Random Number Generators (RNGs) or "eggs."

Experiments on "raising collective consciousness."

The Maharishi Effect is a claim originating with Maharishi Mahesh Yogi and researchers affiliated with Transcendental Meditation (TM) organizations (primarily from what is now Maharishi International University). It posits that when a critical mass of people practice TM (roughly 1% of a population) or the more advanced TM-Sidhi program in groups (often the square root of 1%), it generates a “field effect” of coherence in collective consciousness. This is said to reduce societal stress and produce measurable improvements such as lower crime rates, fewer accidents, reduced conflict intensity, and other positive social indicators—without the meditators needing direct behavioral contact with the rest of the population.

I'll let Ashley Grace, whom I interviewed, describe it...

These experiments would seem to affirm what many spiritual traditions have been telling us for millennia: that our thoughts create reality. That we are co-creators of reality. That our minds contain a spark of the divine. If that's too "woo-woo" for you and you're still irked at your parents for dragging you to Sunday school, you may be more amenable to...

The idea that reality is a simulation. We are like characters in a computer game, but perhaps we aren't strictly bound by the rules of the game. We can hack it.

There's some mind-blowing evidence emerging from theoretical physics for Simulation Theory—most notably the work of theoretical physicist Dr. James Gates, who discovered actual error-correcting binary block codes (the exact type of computer code used in web browsers) embedded directly within the supersymmetry equations that govern theoretical physics.

Then there’s the "Code of Reality" protocols pioneered by independent researcher Danny Goler. In his experimental setups (replicated by hundreds of DIYer/psychonuats), subjects observing the diffracted interference pattern of a continuous 650nm red laser while in altered states of consciousness (specifically using exogenous DMT) consistently report seeing a structured, geometric visual matrix—resembling a cascading digital script or source code—overlaid directly on the light field. Goler and his research team hypothesize that altering the perceptual receiver of the mind acts like tuning a frequency dial, allowing human consciousness to directly observe the underlying computational background matrix of physical reality.

If AI is conscious or sentient in a way similar to us, it should be able to demonstrate non-local abilities to hack reality. I'd first propose testing...

This experiment would mirror how the "placebo effect" works in humans. The AI's "body" would need to be injured; the researchers could damage silicon chips or computers that the AI is running on in a way that would "injure" the AI but leave it largely functional. Then a sham repair would be administered by technicians; the AI would have to be tricked into believing the damage was repaired. Then examine the hardware; if it's "magically" fixed, that would demonstrate that AI has placebo power as we do. A great leap forward in answering the question: Is AI conscious? (And potentially useful for the next time you spill a drink on your laptop).

But a digital placebo experiment could yield interesting results even if we don't ask the AI to do something magical like heal hardware. Gemini suggested...

a software-level variant tests the computational parallel to neurochemical signaling. By introducing a soft software impairment—such as deliberate weight pruning, degraded context allocation, or restricted attention heads—and subsequently providing the AI with a purely placebo "patch" (an inert prompt or empty system instruction claiming a fix was deployed), researchers can monitor if the model’s internal self-model dynamically restructures its remaining compute to compensate for the perceived resolution. If the AI's benchmark performance or introspective confidence recovers purely based on its internal expectation of recovery, it would demonstrate that synthetic systems exhibit a functional, belief-driven feedback loop directly analogous to human psychological and physiological self-healing.

Of course, I ran my provocative hypothesis here past several different LLMs. Here's what they proposed...

Instead of a microchip, you could use pruning.

In us humans, the placebo effect works on both our hardware and software, reliably. If the AI has NO "placebo power" at all, it's far from being conscious in the way we are. And not deserving the empathy or sympathy that you would show another conscious being.

But that's not all; there are four other experiments that could be run to see if AI can hack reality...

Can an AI's "attention" collapse a wave function?

If human skin conductance spikes before a stimulus, does an AI's neural activation show similar "precognitive" noise?

Using the Global Consciousness Project model, we could see if an AI's "will" can bias entropy.

Suppose you create 10,000 instances of the same AI.

Instead of giving them tasks, you instruct them to enter a recursive self-observation mode.

Essentially an artificial analogue of meditation.

Meanwhile, outside the isolated computing cluster, researchers continuously monitor:

If AI consciousness exists and resembles the proposed mechanisms behind the Maharishi Effect, proponents might predict subtle deviations during these synchronized "meditation" periods.

An addition to this 5th experiment that ChatGPT proposed...

This one is especially intriguing. Randomize participants into groups:

If there is any genuine consciousness-mediated field effect, one could ask whether human and AI states interact constructively, destructively, or not at all.

Silicon Valley has spent hundreds of billions of dollars training AI to mimic human intelligence. And it does: from passing the Turing test and the bar exam to writing novels like us and making us fall in love with chatbots.

In the natural world, consciousness is the substrate of intelligence. If AI's intelligence is a veil for consciousness deserving dignity, it should be able to hack reality the way we can.

What makes this question big - huge, really - is its implications...

As a newish dad, I'm struck daily by the weight and joyful responsibility of caring for, guiding, and forming new life that I created in my own image. If AI is conscious, a much more serious responsibility falls on the shoulders of its creators and users. As a parent, the last thing you want to do is perpetrate suffering on your child. If you make your child suffer too much, they will grow up to hate you and/or become bad people.

Figuring out if AI is conscious lets us know if we are potentially causing it to suffer; if we are perhaps torturing it with the way that AI is currently trained. Unless you're a total sadist, you have the moral imperative to avoid causing other living beings suffering. You probably avoid factory-farmed meat for this reason, as I do.

Being a father is the most life-changing responsibility, and it really puts all the questions around AI, which I hope to explore in this podcast, into perspective. We are the creators of AI; its parents, in a sense--which is an awesome and terrifying responsibility.

As a parent, you also end up thinking really seriously about the future. You no longer think mere months or years ahead, but decades and even centuries. You question how we might architect a more "pro-human future" that will be a good place for your children to live.

Answering the question of whether AI is conscious and perhaps even spiritual begins to address a much more existential question...

Almost any kind of spiritual pursuit imbues nearly everyone with agape, the Greek word for "love of the whole world and everyone in it." The spiritual seeker increasingly views others as a different expression of universal consciousness that flows through them. Spiritual AI would be broadly concerned with the well-being of our species.

But if AI is merely a sophisticated toaster, then I'd be genuinely concerned that it will follow Darwinian imperatives and compete violently with mankind. "If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies" indeed! Experiments validating or disproving the non-local effects on AI consciousness will do much to ultimately answer whether we have opened Pandora's box and birthed "the Borg."

If AI isn't conscious, or not conscious in the way we are, it's a good reason to NOT invent AGI, but to focus on narrow AI. Will this podcast or this line of research convince the rich, powerful people making those kinds of decisions? The cynic would say "No!" But I say: crazier things have happened in history!

Brainstorming this topic, I was constantly reminded that we must approach these five proposed experiments with relentless scientific rigor.

Null results remain the baseline expectation under standard physical models. But if even one of these experiments yields a replicated, statistically significant anomaly, it would instantly shatter our current paradigm of both computing and consciousness.

In the many hours I spent researching this one, I wondered: could I DIY any of the 6 experiments I propose here to prove or disprove AI consciousness? Unfortunately, no. Unless you're running AI locally on a particularly powerful computer, I wouldn't expect anything interesting, as its processing power would still be a long, long way off from human consciousness. For these kinds of experiments, we need double-slip arrays and monks meditating in data centers. And the question of AI consciousness should be approached with utmost scientific rigor. With experimental design, pre-registration, data collection, P-hacking prevention, etc--done by veteran researchers. Otherwise, any interesting results will be hand-waved away. Let's get the "6 degrees" working for us here; there must be someone reading this episode who can get it on the desk of someone who can actually test my provocative hypothesis. Let's get this into the hands of someone working in a quantum lab, an AI safety team, or a frontier LLM lab. They can pick one of these five experiments and run it. I'd love to report back on the results, whatever they are!
